title: Chapter 63: Six Clockwork Men, Part 1 of 5: Room Nine
html:
Every morning before the first bell, Wren Halloway carried a tray up to Room Nine and tapped heard on the back of an old soldier's hand.
She had done it every morning since Tuesday. She did it this morning too, the same as always, though nothing else in the house on Steeple Lane was the same as always.
She woke in the dark, in her narrow room behind the study, at the half hour before the first bell, without needing to be woken. She dressed by feel. The white close coat, with its twelve silver buttons, done up to the throat. The white breeches, the white stockings, the black boots. She put up her hair by feel too, in the small cracked glass on the back of the door, though she could not see her face in it in the dark: twisted tight, and pinned, and pinned again, until there was not one fair hair loose to catch the wind. Cadets of the Inquisition did not have loose hair. Kross did not care about such things, as far as she could tell. But she cared. It was the only part of the morning that was all hers.
Then she went down to the kitchen.
The kitchen of the house on Steeple Lane was in the cellar, and it was the only warm room in the house. Everything else was cold and white and scrubbed and empty. The kitchen had a range, a big black iron range that Mrs. Oddie the cook kept going all night, and a scrubbed table, and a dresser with plain white plates on it, and a smell of coal and bread and, always, faintly, peppermint. Kross kept a paper of peppermints on every table in the house, even this one.
Mrs. Oddie had the tray ready. She always did. She was a short wide silent woman with arms like hams, and she had worked for Kross for eighteen years and in all that time, as far as Wren knew, had never asked him a single question. She put the tray on the table without a word. A bowl of porridge with salt on it, not sugar. A mug of tea, strong, with milk. A heel of yesterday's bread. A spoon.
"Thank you, Mrs. Oddie."
Mrs. Oddie nodded.
Wren carried the tray up four flights of stairs in the dark, past the scrubbed pale treads with the dark ring worn into the fifth one, past the study door, past the shut door of the white room on the second floor, and her steps went slower there, as they had every time she passed it since yesterday afternoon. Then on, up, to the top of the house, where the ceilings were low and the doors were plain, and the last door on the left had a number on it, painted small in black on the white: 9.
She knocked. Two, and then three. The pattern Kross had told her to use, so that the man inside would know it was her and not someone else.
Then she opened the door and went in.
Room Nine was small and white, like every room in the house. A bed with a gray blanket. A chair. A window, high up, with bars on the outside, looking over the roofs toward the river. A washstand with a jug. A chamber pot. Nothing on the walls. Nothing on the floor.
Sergeant Ebenezer Moll was sitting on the edge of his bed, waiting for her, with his hands on his knees.
He was always sitting like that when she came in. He never seemed to have been asleep. He was an old man, gray and thin, with a face like a tired hound's, and one leg that did not bend properly at the knee, so that it stuck out stiffly in front of him when he sat. He wore the gray shirt and trousers Kross had given him. His boots were under the bed, side by side, with the laces tucked into them.
He looked at her when she came in. He always looked at her. He did not say anything. He never said anything. Kross had told her, on the first day, that Moll had not spoken a word since they brought him to the house. That he could if he wanted to. That he did not want to.
Wren put the tray on the chair beside the bed.
Then she knelt down on the bare floor in front of him, and took his right hand off his knee, and turned it over so that the back of it was up, and tapped on it with two fingers.
A quick run of taps, and a pause, and a slower run after it, and one last tap on its own.
That was heard. She had learned it from him. Or rather she had learned it from the way his face had changed, on Tuesday morning, the first time Kross had shown her the taps and told her to do them. It meant, as near as she understood it, I am here, and I know you are there, and I have heard you. It was a drum call. A soldier's call, from the war. Kross had told her that, and nothing else.
She tapped it, and stopped, and waited.
Moll's hand lay still under her fingers for a moment.
Then it turned over, slowly, under hers, until her hand was lying in his palm. And his fingers began to tap back.
She knew the first part. Heard. He always tapped heard back. She waited for it to stop, the way it always did.
It did not stop.
His fingers kept moving. On the back of her hand, light and quick and dry, like a bird walking on a roof. A new pattern. Not heard. Something else. She did not know it. Long, and short, and long, and a pause, and a run of quick taps, and two slow ones, and then the long one again, and then stillness.
She looked up at his face.
He was looking at her. His old tired hound's face had not changed. But his eyes were very bright and very steady, and they were holding hers as if he were trying to put something into them.
Then he let go of her hand and put his own back on his knee.
Wren stayed kneeling on the floor for a moment. She looked at the back of her own hand, as if the taps might have left marks.
"I don't know that one," she said. Her voice sounded strange in the small white room. "Sergeant. I don't know what that one means."
Moll did not answer. He never answered.
She got up. She put the spoon in his hand, and the bowl in his lap, the way she did every morning, and he began to eat, slowly, the way he did every morning, and she went out and shut the door.
On the landing outside, she stood still for a long time, with her hand flat on the door.
She would ask someone, she thought. One day. She would ask someone who knew the old drum calls what that one meant.
The Box on the Stair
When she came down from Room Nine, the men were already in the house.
She heard them before she saw them. Low voices on the stair below, and the creak of the treads, and a slow careful bumping, as if something heavy were being carried down a narrow way by people who were afraid of touching the walls. She stopped on the third-floor landing and looked over the banister.
Four men in black were carrying a box down the stair from the second floor.
It was a long box. A plain one, of pale new wood, with rope handles, and a black cloth laid over the top of it and tucked in at the sides. The men carried it on their shoulders, two in front and two behind, and they went down the stair one step at a time, slowly, the front two bending low at the turn so that the box stayed level. They did not speak except to say step and turn and mind.
Wren knew what was in the box.
She had known since yesterday. Since the middle of yesterday afternoon, when she had been standing at the bottom of the stair in the hall, and the girl had come down from the white room with her face like the face of somebody coming down out of a fire, and the harvester had said something to her, very low, at the foot of the stair. Wren had not heard what. She had only seen the girl's face.
And then, after the girl and the harvester had gone, Kross had come down too. He had not gone into his study. He had sat down on the stair, on the fifth step, the one with the dark ring worn into it, with a cup of tea that Mrs. Oddie brought him. And he had stayed there. All evening. All night. Wren knew, because she had sat on the landing above, out of sight, with her knees drawn up, until the second bell after midnight, and he had not moved, and he had not drunk the tea. In the end she had gone to bed. When she got up in the dark this morning, the cup was still on the fifth step, full and cold, with a skin on it.
Lord Aurelian Thorne had died in the white room in the middle of Thursday afternoon, with his daughter's hand under his, tapping. Now four men in black were carrying him down the stair to a cart, to take him to Saint Clement's, to lie in the church there until Sunday.
Wren stood on the landing and watched them go.
She did not know why her throat had gone tight. She had not known him. She had seen him twice. Once, two weeks ago, on a litter, coming up Steeple Lane in the rain with Kross walking beside it, a long gray shape under a blanket with one thin hand outside it, tapping on the litter's edge. And once yesterday, in the white room, through the open door, with his daughter's hand under his.
Twice. That was all. And yet she found she was holding the banister very hard, and that her eyes were stinging, and that she could not have said a word just then if Kross himself had asked her one.
At the bottom of the stair, in the hall, the men stopped. One of them opened the front door. Cold air came in, and gray light, and the sound of a horse stamping in the lane.
Kross was standing in the hall.
He had not changed his clothes. He was in his shirtsleeves still, and his gray waistcoat, unbuttoned, the way he had been yesterday afternoon. His face was gray. Not the gray of the harvester's hands. The gray of a man who has not slept and has not eaten and has sat all night on a cold stair looking at a wall. His hair was not combed. Wren had never seen his hair not combed.
He walked across the hall to the box, and stopped beside it.
The four men in black stood very still, holding the box on their shoulders, and did not look at him.
Kross lifted his right hand. Wren saw that the glove was off. He did not touch the cloth. He held his bare hand just above it, an inch above, flat, palm down, the way you hold your hand over a fire to feel the warmth. He held it there for a long moment.
Then he took it away.
"Gently," he said. Very quietly. "The step is broken at the gate. Mind it."
"Yes, sir."
The men carried the box out into the lane, and the door shut behind them, and the hall was empty except for Kross, standing in the middle of the scrubbed white floor in his shirtsleeves, with his bare hand at his side.
He did not look up. He did not seem to know she was there.
Then, without looking up, he said, "Halloway."
Wren's heart jumped.
"Sir."
"Did he eat?"
She did not understand for a moment. Then she did. "Sergeant Moll? Yes, sir. He's eating now."
"Good." Kross stood for a moment longer. "Good." He turned toward the study, and stopped, and turned back, and looked up the stairwell at her for the first time. His gray eyes were very tired. "You'll go to the Long Office as usual," he said. "I'll be in by the fourth bell."
"Yes, sir."
He went into his study and shut the door.
Wren stood on the landing for a long time. Then she went down. On the fifth step she stopped, and picked up the cold cup of tea with its skin on it, and carried it down to the kitchen, and gave it to Mrs. Oddie without a word, and Mrs. Oddie took it without a word, and poured it away.
Then Wren went out into the lane.
The cart was at the bottom of Steeple Lane, by the broken step at the gate, a plain black cart with a black horse. The men were lifting the box into the back of it. Beyond the cart, beyond the roofs, the white needle of the Spire went up into a gray sky, and the pigeons were coming out of the slots at its top in a gray wheeling cloud, the way they did every morning, and the first bell began to ring.
Wren stood at the top of the lane, in her white coat with its twelve silver buttons, and waited until the cart had gone. Then she walked the other way, down the Hill, toward the Ministry.
The Long Office
The Long Office was on the second floor of the Ministry, on the side that faced Mercer Street, and it was exactly what its name said.
It was long. It ran the whole length of the building, from one end to the other, so long that when you stood at the door at one end, the far wall at the other end looked small and gray and blurred, like a wall seen through rain. Down the middle of it, in two rows, back to back, stood the desks. Forty of them, Wren had been told on her first day, and she had counted them since and it was true. Forty tall sloping wooden desks, each with a stool in front of it and a green-shaded lamp on a brass arm above it and an inkwell sunk into the top of it and a rack of pens. Down both long walls, tall windows looked out over the roofs, and between the windows stood cupboards, black, with brass handles, and on every cupboard there was a number.
It smelled of ink, and dust, and paper, and coal from the four small stoves that stood down the middle of the room between the rows of desks and never quite warmed it. And it sounded, always, of pens. Forty pens, scratching. Sometimes a cough. Sometimes the creak of a stool. Sometimes a clerk getting up and walking down the aisle to one of the black cupboards, and the click of its brass handle. But mostly pens, scratching, on and on, from the first bell to the eighth, like rain on a roof.
At the far end, on its own, behind a glass partition with a door in it, was Kross's office.
The door was shut this morning. The green lamp behind the glass was not lit.
Wren went to her own desk, the thirty-first, on the left-hand row near the far end, close enough to Kross's door that she could hear him if he called. She hung her coat on the hook. She sat. She uncapped her ink. The clerk at the next desk, a thin young man called Sedley with a cold that never went away, sniffed at her by way of good morning, and she nodded to him by way of answer, and they both bent their heads.
The work was copying.
It was always copying. Lists, mostly. Lists of names that came up from the Watch houses and the Intake Hall and the Health and the docks, in bad handwriting on bad paper, and had to be written out again, properly, in the Inquisition's clean black hand, on the Inquisition's good white paper, and filed. Names of people sought. Names of people found. Names of people taken. Names of people released, though there were never many of those. Wren copied them, one after another, line after line, in her small neat hand, and did not think about what they were, because that was how you got through a day in the Long Office. You did not think about what they were.
Today it was hard not to think.
The Thursday list was pinned by the door.
She had seen it as she came in. Everybody saw it. It was pinned on a board just inside the door at the near end, where every clerk had to pass it on the way to their desk, and it was new every Thursday, and every clerk was supposed to read it, so that if a name on it came across their desk during the week, they would know. Wren had read it at the door. She had not meant to stop. She had stopped anyway.
The first name on it was new. It was written larger than the others, at the very top, and underlined.
VANE, CORIN. Harvester, formerly of this Ministry. Lame in the left leg. Gray to the shoulder. To be held on sight. By order of the Inquisitor. S. K.
She had stood in front of it with her coat over her arm until somebody coughed behind her.
Now she sat at her desk and copied names, and the room scratched round her, and she thought about a man with gray hands sitting in a carriage at the bottom of Steeple Lane yesterday, turning a gray stone over in his fingers. A beach stone, with a white line round it. Her stone. The one she had picked up on the shingle below the Fish Stairs when she was a girl and kept in her pocket for years without knowing why, and then given to him, in the autumn, on a night she had lied for him to the man she worked for.
Take it to the Glass, she had told him yesterday. She did not know why she had said it. I think it came from there.
She did not know why she thought that, either.
She dipped her pen and copied another name.
The clerks were talking, a little. Not much. Not loud enough for anyone to be told off. But Wren heard it, under the scratching. Two desks behind her. Three desks in front. Low voices, passing a thing from one to another the way you pass a coal along a line of hands.
...held the roof up, they say, on his knees...
...all that light, my mother saw it from the Saltmarsh...
...the Inquisitor's put him on the list...
...the same one? The harvester?
...gray to the shoulder, it says...
Wren kept her head down.
It was halfway through the morning, at the second bell, when she noticed the silence.
She did not notice it at once. She noticed, first, that the pen at the next desk had stopped. Then that the pens behind her had stopped. Then that the whole of the Long Office had gone quiet, forty pens lying still, forty clerks with their heads half turned, and in the silence there was only one sound.
It was her. She was humming.
Three notes. The same three notes she always hummed, the ones that came out of her when she was copying and not thinking, the ones she did not know the name of or where she had learned them. Up, and up, and up a little more, and then nothing, a sort of waiting space where the fourth note ought to be and was not. She had been humming them over and over, under her breath, while she wrote, and she had not heard herself at all.
She stopped.
Forty faces looked at her for a moment longer. Then, one by one, they looked away again, and bent their heads, and the pens began to scratch.
Wren sat with her face burning.
At the desk across the aisle from hers, a tall young man in a cadet's black coat had not bent his head. He was sitting very still with his pen held above his paper, and he was looking at her, and his face was white.
Rowan Thorne.
She had forgotten he would be here. He came on Fridays, for his copying duty, the way all the Academy cadets did. She had not thought he would come today. His father had died yesterday afternoon in a white room four streets away. His father was lying in a cart, now, on the way to Saint Clement's.
And he had come to the Long Office anyway, and sat down at his desk, and uncapped his ink, and was copying names.
He was looking at her as if she had hit him.
Wren looked back at him. She did not know what to say. She did not know what she had done. She thought, from the look on his face, that he did not know either.
Then he bent his head, very quickly, and began to write, and his pen moved fast and hard across the paper, and did not stop again for a long time.
